blocks.p: "His brother," Rei said aloud. His voice came out small and flat in the not-air, the voice of a man in a kitchen. "I'm his brother. That's all I am."

blocks.cap: Rei before the man of light

blocks.p: The chair did not answer that. Behind it the man of light did not move. Kuga's eyes held his, yellow and patient, and Rei felt the cat beginning to tire in his arms, a faint restlessness in the weight, the first warning. He did not have long. He had one question. Gin's book had been very clear on the number.

He had spent the walk from Kita deciding what to ask. How to save Gin. How to close the wall. How to kill the thing in his brother's body. Each of them was a question about power, and he had a feeling, standing here, that power was the one thing this man had stopped hearing about centuries ago. So he asked the other one. The one his brother had drowned to point him at.
"Who were you?"
The light flinched.

It was not much. A ripple through the cold shine of him, the way a candle flame dips when a door opens somewhere in the house. The man did not turn. But his head moved, a fraction, toward one shoulder, the way a person half turns when he hears his name called in a crowd and is not sure it was meant for him. And the answer came into Rei the way the lattice had given him its history. Not in words. In pieces, out of order, like photographs dropped on a floor.

A paper lantern at dusk, hanging from a wooden eave, with three characters brushed on it in old ink. 逢魔時. Ōmagatoki. The twilight hour. The hour when a person meets demons. Under the characters was a small crest, plain as an office seal.

A notebook in a young man's hand, its pages full of names written very small, the way Gin wrote the things the records must never see. The hand was ink-stained at the second finger. It turned a page and kept writing. Somebody who asked questions for a living and wrote down the answers.
A city of wooden bridges and low tiled roofs, of carts and sandals and swords worn at the hip. No wires. No neon. A river with no concrete on its banks. Tokyo, before it was called Tokyo.

A narrow road at evening, and the young man walking it with his shadow beside him, not behind. He did not cut it off. He did not follow it either. He walked between the light and the dark the way a person walks along the top of a wall, and the shadow kept pace with him like a companion he had stopped being afraid of.
A plain wooden chair at the centre of everything. The young man sitting down in it, slowly, the way a person sits after a long day. The weight settling onto his shoulders. And him not getting up.

And last, smallest, a single character, like a rivet driven through all the rest. 要. It meant the pivot. The keystone. The pin a folding fan turns on. Rei did not know why it was there. He only knew that the man of light had held it out to him the way a person holds out the one thing he has left in his pocket.

Then the pieces stopped. Behind the chair the man's head turned back to the wall, to the work, to the thing he was holding shut, and the light closed over the place where he had almost been someone. Rei felt it like a door shutting in another room. He had been answered. One question, one answer. That was the rule.
And then the chair let him reach.

That was the cruelty of it. It let his hand close the last of the distance. It let his living fingers find the edge of the vacancy, where the last holder of the Thirteenth had died out of the seat and left it ringing. For one whole second he was touching the wound the way he had wanted to touch his brother all month, directly, with no glass between. In that second he read it. It was not a hole. It was a hand-shaped absence. The negative of a holder who had been Duty and something else besides, two paths braided into one law, the way Rei's own two were braided, unspoken, inside him. He understood, all at once and far too late, why the Healer had wanted him here and not only the chair. Why it had offered him the seat in his own kitchen, as mercy. The wound was keyed to a soul that walked more than one path. It had been waiting six years and longer for the right shape of hand. And the hand it had been waiting for was, near enough, his.
Then the far shore decided what he was. What he was was alive. And it did to him what a body does to a splinter.

There was no anger in it. That was the part he would never be able to explain afterwards, the part that would sit under his breastbone for the rest of the month. There was only the vast, patient correction of a place expelling the one thing in it that breathed. The standing turned. The whole leaning field of attention that had faced the centre faced him instead, all at once, without swinging. The not-weather went from thick to total. And the chair, the plain kitchen chair, the loudest quiet he had ever stood near, pushed. Not with force he could brace against. With ending. With the flat refusal of a closed door that has decided a man was never inside.
Kuga looked away.

The door shut at once, the way the page had promised, no warning, no grace. Rei was thrown back along Gin's order in reverse and far too fast. All the half steps he had walked so carefully were spent in one backward fall. The streets got their lettering back and their depth and their lying conviction in strobe as he went. Canal. Konbini. Lantern. The stranger's eyes peeled off the back of his neck a layer at a time. And the last thing the far shore did, as it shut behind him, was close its hand. He felt it close around the part of him that had touched the wound. He felt the wound hold on. And he felt it tear. Not his skin, nothing so simple. It tore the way a name tears when two people are saying it at once.

He came out of the water on his back. The settling pool slapped up around him in a sheet and came down on his face, warm, stinking of iron and river. Okada's hand was already there, under his head, keeping his mouth above the surface. Somewhere to his left a cat was complaining loudly about being wet.
"Breathe," Okada said. "Rei. Breathe first."

He breathed. The real August heat sat on him. The real security lights buzzed. Somewhere beyond the pump house the real lanterns of somebody's okuribi were swinging on a real string. He lay on the lip of the pool in his own moving world and looked at his hands. They had come back with him. They were no longer only his hands.
At the yard gate the rat snake struck.

It hit the empty air over the sill so fast that Rei only saw the end of it, the long pale body snapping back into its coil. Okada was on her feet. Nothing came through the gate. The snake's head stayed fixed on the space above the grave-earth, tongue going, and after a long minute it slowly lowered its chin to the concrete again.

Okada crouched beside it and laid two fingers along its back, and her eyes went unfocused. Rei had seen her do the same to a stack of files. "Small," she said at last. "Low class. It came up the trace behind you, the way water comes up a footprint. It tried the gate and the snake bit it and it went back down." She took her fingers away and looked at him, and for once she did not look at his hands first. "It followed you out, Rei. Something over there has your smell now."

His hands looked like his hands until they didn't. In the security light they were only hands, scraped at the heel from the concrete lip, shaking the ordinary way a man shakes after a fall. Then he turned them over and the marks were there. Faint as the afterimage of a window stared at too long, laid into the lines of his palms like a second set of prints under the first. He knew without being told that they were not decoration and not injury. They were the grain of the wound, printed onto the hand that had touched it. And under the grain, finer still, something else. The leftover warmth of the man at the centre, who had every path there was lit inside him to its ceiling, and who had answered Rei's question with a hand held out.
He flexed his fingers, and one of the lines warmed.

For half a heartbeat he heard a woman. Not with his ears. She was old, two floors up in the dark block across the road, lying awake on a futon, and the thought came into him whole and tired and not his. I never can sleep at Obon. He always comes and stands at the foot of the bed. Then she was gone. Rei had read people all his life, but only the space around them, the surface of the lake. Gin's book had a line for the difference. A Clairsentient knows you are angry. A Telepath knows why. That had not been the surface. That had been the water.
He stood up too fast, and the world skipped.

blocks.cap: A teleport flicker that is not his

blocks.p: One moment he was on his feet at the edge of the pool. The next he was three metres along it, by the pump-house wall, with nothing in between. No step. No sense of moving. Just here, and then there, and a hard sick lurch in his stomach as if he had missed a stair in the dark. Behind him on the wet concrete his footprints ran from the pool's edge and stopped, and then there was dry concrete, and then there was him.
Okada stared at the gap in the footprints. Kuga stopped washing and stared too.
"That isn't yours," Okada said quietly.
"I know."

It frightened him more than the shove had. The shove had been a door closing. This was a door left open inside his own skin. He had spent his whole life with two paths held down so far he had taught himself they were one, because the one he let himself have was easier to carry than the truth of both. And now there was a third thing in his hands that was not even his. Abilities he had not earned and could not give back, firing on their own, and under them a grain keyed to a seat that had been waiting for exactly the hand he had.

He understood the trap completely now, the way a person understands a sentence the instant after he has said the wrong half of it. The Healer had never needed to make him take the chair. It had only needed him to touch the wound. The far shore had done the rest. It had marked him and keyed him and begun the long quiet work of making his hand fit the absence. The borrowed sparks would burn out. He could feel that already, the way he could feel a fever deciding to break. But the grain under them would not. It would get a little more his every day he carried it, a little less borrowed, until the difference between holding the seat and being the kind of thing that holds it was a difference he could no longer find.

He closed his fists over the marks, and they pulsed against his palms. Patient. Not his. Getting his. Down the river the real lanterns swung on their string, and the real heat sat on the real water, and the city breathed around him, asleep and unaware. And somewhere under all of it, leaning on a wall that rang with the shape of an empty kitchen chair, his brother was being worn by something that had just got everything it sent him in to get.

He had come back from beyond the veil alive, which no one was supposed to do. He had come back knowing where the wound was and how it tore. He had come back with a lantern, a notebook, a road, a chair and one small character he could not read the meaning of. And he had come back carrying the first instalment of the price, printed into the only hands he had ever had to reach for Gin with. Standing by the pool with his fists shut, he did not know whether he had brought home the way to close the wall, or only the wall's way of choosing him.
